name: Steer pods with nodeSelector & taints
objective: CKA › Workloads & Scheduling. Drill EVERY way to control where pods land, harder than the exam: node labels + nodeSelector, taints & tolerations (Equal + Exists), required and preferred nodeAffinity, pod anti-affinity spread, manual nodeName scheduling, DaemonSet coverage, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix for an unschedulable pod. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Label a node + nodeSelector
questions.teach:
`spec.nodeSelector` is the simplest placement control: the pod only lands on a node whose labels contain **every** key/value listed (exact equality, AND'ed). Label a node with `kubectl label node <node> key=value`.

**Gotcha:** if no node carries the label, the pod sits `Pending` forever — check `kubectl describe pod` events.
questions.prompt:
Worker node `$W1` exists. Label it `disktype=ssd`, then in namespace `sched-learn` create pod `ssd-pod` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) with `nodeSelector` `disktype=ssd`.  Give  a toleration for  so it still lands on  after that node is tainted.

Target: `ssd-pod` is `Running` and its `.spec.nodeName` is the node you labeled `disktype=ssd`.
questions.hint: `kubectl label node "$W1" disktype=ssd`, then set `spec.nodeSelector.disktype: ssd` on the pod.
questions.solution:
kubectl label node "$W2" disktype=ssd --overwrite
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ssd-pod
  namespace: sched-learn
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    disktype: ssd
  tolerations:
  - key: workload
    operator: Equal
    value: batch
    effect: NoSchedule
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF

verification.description: ssd-pod Running on a disktype=ssd node via nodeSelector

questions.eli5:
Imagine the cluster is a big parking lot, and your pod is a car looking for a spot (a node).

- **Labels** are coloured stickers you put on parking spots. You can stick a blue **"ssd"** sticker on one spot: `kubectl label node <node> disktype=ssd`.
- **nodeSelector** is you telling the car: *"only park in a spot that has the blue ssd sticker."* The car drives around and parks on the first spot that has it.

That's the whole idea: label the node, then ask the pod to only go where that label exists.

**But watch out:**

- If **no spot** has the sticker, the car just idles forever — the pod stays `Pending`. It will **not** settle for a different spot. Run `kubectl describe pod <name>` and read the **Events** at the bottom; it'll say something like *"didn't match node selector."*
- You can ask for **more than one sticker** (`disktype=ssd` **and** `zone=a`). Then the car only parks where **all** of them are present — it's "AND", never "any of".
- Stickers must match **exactly**. `ssd` ≠ `SSD` ≠ `solid-state`. One typo and nothing matches.
- A nodeSelector only picks a spot *by sticker*. It does **not** get you past a "Reserved" sign (a **taint**) on that spot — that needs a **toleration** (the next step).
questions.deepDive:
## Node labels + nodeSelector — full rundown

### What it is
`nodeSelector` is the **simplest** way to constrain which nodes a pod may run on. You put labels on nodes, then list required labels on the pod. The scheduler only considers nodes whose labels are a **superset** of what the pod asks for.

- Matching is **exact key=value equality**, and multiple entries are **AND-ed** (every one must match).
- There is no "OR", no "not equal", no ranges — for any of that you need **nodeAffinity** (a later lesson).

### The commands
```bash
# label a node
kubectl label node <node> disktype=ssd

# overwrite an existing label (fails without --overwrite if the key already exists)
kubectl label node <node> disktype=ssd --overwrite

# remove a label (trailing minus)
kubectl label node <node> disktype-

# see a node's labels
kubectl get node <node> --show-labels
kubectl get nodes -L disktype          # show the disktype label as its own column
```

On the pod:
```yaml
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    disktype: ssd
```

### How the match works
| Pod asks for | Node has | Lands? |
|---|---|---|
| `disktype=ssd` | `disktype=ssd` | ✅ |
| `disktype=ssd` | `disktype=ssd, zone=a` | ✅ (node can have extra labels) |
| `disktype=ssd, zone=a` | `disktype=ssd` | ❌ (missing `zone=a`) |
| `disktype=ssd` | `disktype=SSD` | ❌ (case/value differs) |
| `disktype=ssd` | *(no such label anywhere)* | ❌ → pod `Pending` |

### Built-in labels you can select on
Every node already carries well-known labels you can target without creating any:

- `kubernetes.io/hostname` — the node's name
- `kubernetes.io/os` — `linux` / `windows`
- `kubernetes.io/arch` — `amd64` / `arm64`
- `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane` — present on control-plane nodes
- `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, `topology.kubernetes.io/region` — cloud topology

### nodeSelector vs nodeAffinity
`nodeSelector` is a subset of what affinity can do. Reach for **nodeAffinity** when you need:
- "In" a set of values (`disktype in (ssd, nvme)`)
- `NotIn` / `Exists` / `DoesNotExist`
- **preferred** (soft) rules — "try, but don't block scheduling"

`nodeSelector` is always **hard/required**: no node → `Pending`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No matching node → `Pending` forever.** Diagnose with `kubectl describe pod <name>` → *Events* → *"0/N nodes are available: … didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector."*
- nodeSelector **does not beat a taint.** If the only matching node is tainted, you also need a matching **toleration**, or the pod still won't land.
- Labels are **cluster-wide and mutable**: relabelling a node can strand or move pods on the next (re)schedule.
- `kubectl run --overrides` or editing a running pod's `nodeSelector` isn't allowed — most pod fields are immutable; recreate the pod instead.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl label node $W1 disktype=ssd --overwrite
kubectl run ssd-pod --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"disktype":"ssd"}}}' \
  --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod ssd-pod -o wide          # confirm NODE == $W1
```

questions.title: Taint a node + matching toleration
questions.teach:
A **taint** repels pods that don't tolerate it: `kubectl taint node <node> key=value:NoSchedule`. A pod opts in with a `toleration` whose `key`/`value`/`effect` match (operator `Equal`).

**Gotcha:** a toleration only *permits* the node, it doesn't *attract* — pair it with `nodeSelector`/affinity to actually land there.
questions.prompt:
Taint node `$W2` with `workload=batch:NoSchedule`. Then in `sched-learn` create pod `batch-pod` (`busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`) that **tolerates** that taint (operator `Equal`) AND uses `nodeSelector disktype=ssd` so it lands on `$W2`.

Target: `$W2` carries the taint and `batch-pod` is `Running` on `$W2` with a matching toleration.
questions.hint: `kubectl taint node "$W2" workload=batch:NoSchedule`. Toleration `{key: workload, operator: Equal, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule}` plus `nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd}`.
questions.solution:
kubectl taint node "$W2" workload=batch:NoSchedule --overwrite
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: batch-pod
  namespace: sched-learn
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    disktype: ssd
  tolerations:
  - key: workload
    operator: Equal
    value: batch
    effect: NoSchedule
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF

verification.description: $W1 tainted workload=batch:NoSchedule and batch-pod Running there with matching toleration

questions.eli5:
A **taint** is a "Keep Out" sign you stick on a node. By default every pod reads the sign and stays away. A **toleration** is a little pass a pod carries that says *"I'm allowed past this exact sign."*

Think of a node as a **VIP room**:

- `kubectl taint node X key=value:NoSchedule` hangs a velvet rope + sign on room **X**.
- A pod with a matching **toleration** is on the guest list — it's *allowed* in.
- Everyone **without** the matching pass is turned away at that room.

The most important thing to understand: being *allowed* in is **not** the same as being *sent* in. 👉 A toleration only lets a pod **ignore** the sign — it does **not** drag the pod to that room. If you actually want the pod to go there, you also have to **point** it there with a `nodeSelector` or affinity.

The sign comes in **three strengths**:

- **NoSchedule** — "no new guests without a pass." (Pods already inside get to stay.)
- **PreferNoSchedule** — "please avoid this room, but if there's nowhere else, fine."
- **NoExecute** — "everybody without a pass, OUT — right now." (This one even **kicks out** pods that are already running.)

**Watch out for:**

- **Toleration ≠ attraction.** A toleration alone can still let the pod land on *any other* node. Pair it with `nodeSelector` to force the room.
- The **control-plane node** has a built-in Keep Out sign — that's why your normal pods never land on it.
- **NoExecute** evicts running pods; the other two only affect *new* pods being scheduled.
- To **take the sign down**, repeat the command with a **trailing dash**: `kubectl taint node X key=value:NoSchedule-`.
questions.deepDive:
## Taints & tolerations — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
**Taints repel. Tolerations permit. Affinity/nodeSelector attract.**
A taint on a node keeps pods *off* unless the pod carries a matching toleration — and even then, a toleration only *allows* the node, it never *pulls* the pod toward it.

### Anatomy of a taint
A taint is three parts: **`key=value:effect`**.
```bash
kubectl taint node <node> workload=batch:NoSchedule
#                          └ key ┘ └value┘ └ effect ┘
```
- `value` is optional: `kubectl taint node <node> dedicated:NoSchedule` (key-only taint).
- A node can hold **many** taints; a pod must tolerate **every** taint that applies to be schedulable there.

### The three effects
| Effect | New pods without a toleration | Already-running pods without a toleration |
|---|---|---|
| **NoSchedule** | ❌ not scheduled here | ✅ stay (untouched) |
| **PreferNoSchedule** | ⚠️ avoided if possible, else allowed | ✅ stay |
| **NoExecute** | ❌ not scheduled here | ❌ **evicted** |

`NoExecute` is the only effect that touches running pods.

### Managing taints
```bash
# add
kubectl taint node $W2 workload=batch:NoSchedule

# change an existing taint's value/effect
kubectl taint node $W2 workload=batch:NoSchedule --overwrite

# REMOVE — note the trailing dash
kubectl taint node $W2 workload=batch:NoSchedule-

# inspect
kubectl describe node $W2 | grep -A1 Taints
kubectl get node $W2 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'; echo
```

### Anatomy of a toleration (on the pod)
```yaml
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: workload
    operator: Equal        # Equal (default) or Exists
    value: batch           # only with operator: Equal
    effect: NoSchedule     # match a specific effect, or omit to tolerate ALL effects of this key
    # tolerationSeconds: 300   # only meaningful with effect: NoExecute
```

### operator: Equal vs Exists
- **`Equal`** (default): `key`, `value`, and `effect` must all match the taint.
- **`Exists`**: match on `key` (+ optional `effect`), **ignore value**. Do **not** set `value` with `Exists`.
- **Tolerate everything** (used by system agents / DaemonSets):
  ```yaml
  tolerations:
  - operator: Exists      # no key, no effect → tolerates every taint on every node
  ```
- An **empty `effect`** with a given key tolerates **all effects** of that key (NoSchedule *and* NoExecute).

### tolerationSeconds (NoExecute only)
How long a tolerating pod may **stay** on a node after a `NoExecute` taint appears before it's evicted. `0` or unset-with-no-toleration → evicted immediately; a value → grace period. This is the mechanism behind the 5-minute "node not-ready" eviction (see below).

### Well-known / built-in taints
Kubernetes adds these automatically — knowing them explains a lot of "why won't my pod land here" behaviour:

| Taint | When | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane` | on control-plane nodes | `NoSchedule` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/not-ready` | node not Ready | `NoExecute` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/unreachable` | node controller lost contact | `NoExecute` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure` | low memory | `NoSchedule` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure` | low disk | `NoSchedule` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/pid-pressure` | PID exhaustion | `NoSchedule` |
| `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable` | node cordoned | `NoSchedule` |

> The scheduler auto-adds 300s tolerations for `not-ready` and `unreachable` to most pods — that's the ~5-minute delay before pods are evicted from a dead node.

### Taints + attraction, together
A toleration lets a pod *onto* a tainted node but doesn't send it there. To **dedicate** a node to certain pods, combine both:
1. **Taint** the node so random pods stay off: `dedicated=team-a:NoSchedule`.
2. On the special pods, add a **matching toleration** *and* a **nodeSelector**/affinity for a label on that node.

Without the nodeSelector, the tolerating pod is merely *allowed* on the node — it may still schedule elsewhere.

### DaemonSets
DaemonSet pods automatically get tolerations for most node-condition taints so they run **everywhere**, including control-plane and pressured nodes. That's why `kube-proxy`/CNI pods appear on every node.

### Debugging
Pod stuck `Pending`?
```bash
kubectl describe pod <name> | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
# "0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {workload: batch}, ..."
```
That message names the exact taint you're missing a toleration for.

### Exam traps
- **Added a toleration but the pod still isn't on the tainted node?** You forgot it doesn't *attract* — add a `nodeSelector`/affinity.
- **`Exists` with a `value`** is invalid. Drop `value` for `Exists`.
- **Removing a taint** needs the trailing `-` *and* the matching `effect`.
- **NoExecute** will evict pods you didn't intend to move — scope it carefully.
- A pod needs to tolerate **all** taints on a node, not just one.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl taint node $W2 workload=batch:NoSchedule
```
```yaml
spec:
  nodeSelector: { disktype: ssd }     # attract to the node
  tolerations:                        # permit the taint
  - { key: workload, operator: Equal, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule }
```

questions.title: Manual scheduling with nodeName
questions.teach:
Setting `spec.nodeName` directly **bypasses the scheduler** — the kubelet on that exact node picks the pod up and runs it. Use it to pin a pod deterministically or when the scheduler is unavailable.

**Gotcha:** a wrong/nonexistent node name does **not** error — the pod sits `Pending` with no scheduler event, since no scheduler ever looked at it.
questions.prompt:
In `sched-learn` create pod `manual-pod` (`busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`) bound to worker `$W2` **via `spec.nodeName`** (no nodeSelector/affinity).

Target: `manual-pod` is `Running` and `.spec.nodeName` == `$W2`.
questions.hint: Put `nodeName: <the $W2 node name>` in `spec`. Find the exact name with `kubectl get nodes`.
questions.solution:
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: manual-pod
  namespace: sched-learn
spec:
  nodeName: $W2
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF

verification.description: manual-pod Running and pinned to $W2 via nodeName

questions.eli5:
Normally the **scheduler** is like the host at a restaurant who decides which table (node) your party (pod) sits at — checking which tables are free, big enough, and not "reserved."

Setting **`spec.nodeName`** is you walking straight in and **sitting at a specific table yourself**, skipping the host entirely. The waiter at that exact table (the node's **kubelet**) just picks you up and starts serving.

**Watch out for:**

- **Typos are silent.** If you name a table that doesn't exist, nobody shouts — the pod just sits `Pending` with **no Events**, because the host (scheduler) was never involved to complain. (With a normal pod, the scheduler *would* leave an event explaining why.)
- **It ignores the rules the host checks.** `nodeName` skips taints, `nodeSelector`, affinity, and resource "does it fit?" checks. The pod can land somewhere it really shouldn't — or get stuck if the node can't actually run it.
- Use it for **emergencies** (scheduler is down) or **absolute pinning**. It's a blunt tool — not something you'd use for everyday scheduling.
questions.deepDive:
## Manual scheduling with nodeName — full rundown

### What it is
`spec.nodeName` hard-binds a pod to one specific node **by name**. When it's set, the default scheduler is **bypassed entirely** — the kubelet on that node sees a pod already assigned to it and starts the containers.

```yaml
spec:
  nodeName: kindlab-worker2
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
```

### How normal scheduling differs
| Step | Normal pod | `nodeName` set |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduler picks a node | ✅ filters + scores all nodes | ❌ skipped |
| Taints (`NoSchedule`) checked | ✅ | ❌ ignored |
| `nodeSelector` / affinity checked | ✅ | ❌ ignored |
| Resource "does it fit" check | ✅ (at schedule time) | ❌ not pre-checked |
| Who sets `.spec.nodeName` | the scheduler | **you** |

### When to use it
- The **scheduler is unavailable** and you must place a pod anyway.
- You need **deterministic, absolute** placement and don't want the scheduler second-guessing.
- Understanding **static pods**: the kubelet runs manifests from `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` with `nodeName` effectively pinned to that node — same bypass mechanism.

### What it does NOT skip
- **`NoExecute` taints still evict it.** Those are enforced by the node/taint-manager after the fact, not the scheduler — so a `nodeName` pod on a `NoExecute`-tainted node can still be kicked off.
- **The kubelet can still reject it.** If the node genuinely can't fit the pod (insufficient CPU/memory), the kubelet may fail it with `OutOfcpu`/`OutOfmemory` rather than it running happily.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Wrong/nonexistent node name = silent `Pending`.** No scheduler → **no scheduling Events**. `kubectl describe pod` shows nothing useful; check the name against `kubectl get nodes`.
- `nodeName` must be the **exact** node name (e.g. `kindlab-worker2`), not a label or hostname guess.
- Most pod fields including `nodeName` are **immutable** once created — fix a typo by deleting and recreating the pod.
- Prefer `nodeSelector`/affinity for real workloads; reserve `nodeName` for pinning and break-glass.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl get nodes                       # copy the exact node name
kubectl run manual-pod --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeName":"'"$W2"'"}}' \
  --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod manual-pod -o wide      # NODE == $W2, no scheduler involved
```
